question: Who has cracked the Panini code in his thesis?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Rishi Rajpopat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rishi Rajpopat, a Sanskrit scholar** of Indian origin who has successfully decoded a complex rule instituted by Panini.
 
• Panini was an ancient scholar considered to be the **father of linguistics**, who lived around 2500 years ago.
 
• Rajpopat's accomplishment is encapsulated in his academic thesis, **'In Panini, We Trust: Discovering the Algorithm for Rule Conflict Resolution in the Astadhyayi'**. 
 
• This groundbreaking work has reportedly resolved a problem that perplexed Sanskrit scholars for centuries, offering some groundbreaking insights into the algorithmic organization of the ancient language.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Panini’s system – 4,000 rules** detailed in the **Astadhyayi**, which was written around **500 BC** – is meant to work like a machine.
 
• Feed in the **base and suffix of a word** and it should turn them into **grammatically correct words and sentences** through a step-by-step process.
 
• Until now, however, there has been a big problem. Often, two or more of Panini’s rules are simultaneously applicable at the same step leaving scholars to agonise over which one to choose.
 
• Solving so-called **“rule conflicts”**, which affect millions of Sanskrit words including certain forms of “mantra” and “guru”, requires an algorithm. 
 
• Rajpopat’s research shows that Panini’s so-called language machine is also self-sufficient.
